messages.subject: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.subject_clean: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

I am new to secr and would like to generate population statistics for a spotted hyena dataset collected using camera traps. I have written and run the code but my results are not intuitive or comparable to a parallel analysis I ran in Program CAPTURE. The secr analysis returns a density of 5.5 hyenas per ha which is significantly different to the 0.00233 animals per ha that I got from CAPTURE. Attached are the input files and R code that I used and a Word file with highlighted screenshots of the R output that I find need help with for your reference.

Kind regards,
Allan.

messages.subject: Re: Uneven sampling - New to SECR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

Thank you so much for your help! I really appreciate it. I reran it using all the traps and the trap locations as the detector instead other the transect marker. The density estimates only changed very slightly so that's great! I decided not to include the juveniles as some of them are likely to disperse around the end of the date and just want to be 100% sure the population is closed.

Thanks!

Nicola

On Sunday, March 20, 2022 at 12:49:25 AM UTC-6 murray...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Nicola
> What a neat study animal! And sorry for delay - the notification went to Spam for some reason.
>
> 1) Go ahead and use all the traps.
> 2) I think two traps at each site should be fine; be sure to record the actual trap that caught an animal, or perhaps assign randomly if that info was lost.
> 3) whether you include juveniles will depend on biology we don't know. At the least, they should be moving independently of their mother. Then the question is whether their behaviour leads to a different detection function (e.g., because less mobile). If you suspect a difference you can check by fitting an individual covariate ('A','J') and using CL = TRUE in secr.fit; compare by AIC with no-age model.
>
> Murray
> On Friday, March 11, 2022 at 2:00:10 PM UTC+13 guthri...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi everyone!
> >
> > As mentioned in the title, I am new to SECR and just starting to analyse my capture-recapture data on mouse lemurs. I have been reading up on using this analysis and want to make sure I'm able to use as much of my data as possible but I have slightly uneven sampling due to two different chapters of my PhD thesis. I'm in an Anthropology department and nobody else studies anything similar so struggling a little bit with some of the basics and I'd appreciate any help.
> >
> > I set up a grid of 5 transects, 300m in length, in a forest fragment. The first transect had 2 Sherman traps set up every 25m but the remaining 4 transects only had 1 trap every 50m. I am using the grid to calculate home range size and was limited by the number of traps I could afford. The first transect is being used in occupancy analysis as I have a further 68 transects spread (all at least 300m apart) throughout the landscape in different land cover types (agriculture, reforestation etc) that have traps every 25m which is why it's slightly different.
> >
> > So my questions are:
> > 1) Is it ok to use all the data collected on the transects in the grid even if some transects had more traps than others or should I reduce the data for the first transect to be the same as the other 4 transects?
> > 2) If I can keep all the trap points from the first transect, is it ok to have two different trap IDs but at the same location? Or should I have my "Detector" as the transect marker e.g. T1-100m (or a numerical code I create for it) instead of the trap number e.g. A15? I have two captures from different dates at the same transect marker but in two different trap numbers from my first transect.
> > 3) Should I only use adults in the analysis or can I include juveniles that were captured?
> >
> > I don't have that many captures (39 individuals, with 39 recaptures (range: 2-7 captures) of 12 individuals) so I'm a little worried about removing too much data. I've already removed a few months of data to be sure I'm keeping it as a closed population.
> >
> > Sorry, this is a bit long for something that is probably rather simple. I'm just trying to be as thorough as possible.
> >
> > Again, I'd really appreciate any help!
> >
> > Thanks,
> >
> > Nicola

messages.subject: Re: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.subject_clean: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.body_plain:
Hello Allan

Ahh. Your R code analyses 'captdata' that is a builtin dataset with simulated animals at about 5.5/ha (see ?captdata)! I also find two probably typos in TrapSECR.txt (missing initial 3 of x-coordinates T13, T72). And you will need a much larger buffer (I suggest 20000). Then

MalHyena.0 <- secr.fit (MalHyena, model = list(g0 ~ 1), buffer = 20000, details=list(fastproximity = FALSE))
 predict(MalHyena.0)
       link     estimate  SE.estimate          lcl          ucl
D       log 1.226085e-03 2.392799e-04 8.393676e-04 1.790974e-03
g0    logit 2.665433e-02 5.931733e-03 1.719303e-02 4.110439e-02
sigma   log 5.085863e+03 6.426653e+02 3.974019e+03 6.508777e+03

I used fastproximity=FALSE as it looks like you will want to compare models with time-varying probabilities.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray

Thanks so much for your help, very much appreciated. I reran the analysis using the code specifications you provided in your response and reproduced the same result.
However, given a study area size of 490 km2, I feel that a buffer of 20000 (i.e. 20 km) would make the effective sampled area too big resulting in an underestimate of the density. Specifying a buffer of 2000 (i.e. a strip of 2 km around the trapping array) would be more realistic but returns the following message:

Warning messages:
1: In bias. D(buffer, temptrps, detectfn = output$detectfn, detectpar = dpar,  :
  bias. D() does not allow for variable effort (detector usage)
2: In buffer bias check (output, buffer, bias Limit) :
  predicted relative bias exceeds 0.01 with buffer = 2000

A buffer of 20000 gives a density of 12.26 hyenas/100 km2 (which seems like an underestimate) while that of 2000 gives a density of 21.67 animals/100 km2, which I believe is more practical and comparable to the Program CAPTURE estimate of 23.27 hyenas/100 km2.
Does the above warning message render the result technically incorrect?

Regards,
Allan.

messages.subject: Re: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.subject_clean: Help with model fitting in secr
messages.body_plain:
CAPTURE does not have a reliable method for estimating density from your data, so the comparison is unhelpful. Your animals are very mobile so you need a large buffer unless there is a known boundary to the habitat. See secr-habitatmasks.pdf <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-habitatmasks.pdf>. The buffer does _not_ define an ETA.

Hi all,

is anyone can help me to fix this error when I try to import a shapefile that I want to use in my density estimation?

 library(sf)
> shppiana <- system.file("Piana_Poly.shp", package = "secr")
> piana <- st_read(shppiana)
Error: `dsn` must point to a source, not an empty string.

I suppose that the problem is when I use system.file
But also I don't understand why the function st_read doesn't work.

Thank you

Emiliano

Emiliano
system.file(..., package="secr")  will only get you files that are distributed with the package.
Compare

> system.file("Piana_Poly.shp", package = "secr")

[1] ""
>system.file("extdata/possumarea.shp", package = "secr")
[1] "C:/R/R-4.0.5/library/secr/extdata/possumarea.shp"

Just give st_read the (full) file name you want to read.

Murray

messages.subject: Running scenarios with different trap layouts using trapsindex
messages.subject_clean: Running scenarios with different trap layouts using trapsindex
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have come across a small problem when using secrdesign. When exploring different trap designs using ‘trapsindex’ in make.scenarios , I get a different estimated density than if I run each trap design individually (an example code and results below - the replicates are set very low for speed while testing but I had the same difference when using more replicates). In the results below I expected the ‘sims1’ output to match the second ‘sims2’ output (underlined), as they are both 8x8 grids with all scenario parameters the same. I thought it may be variation due to it being simulation based but I get consistent results when running it multiple times. I feel like I’m missing something very obvious so any help would be very much appreciated! It would be great to know I don't need to run each design individually.

Code:

detectors <- list(grid6x6 = make.grid(nx=6, ny=6, spacing=35, detector = 'count'),

                              grid8x8 = make.grid(nx=8, ny=8, spacing=35, detector = 'count'))

s1<-make.scenarios(trapsindex = 2, noccasions = 4, D = 5, g0 = 0.2, sigma = 20, crosstraps=FALSE)

s2<-make.scenarios(trapsindex = 1:2, noccasions = 4, D = 5, g0 = 0.2, sigma = 20, crosstraps=FALSE)

sims1 <- run.scenarios(nrepl = 5, trapset = detectors, scenarios = s1, seed = 345, fit = T)

sims2 <- run.scenarios(nrepl = 5, trapset = detectors, scenarios = s2, seed = 345, fit = T)

summary(sims1)

summary(sims2)

Results:

sims1 output: 8x8 grid

                               n             mean                    se

estimate              5             5.00154                0.39745

SE.estimate        5             0.98489                0.05936

lcl                           5             3.41435                0.30984

messages.subject: telemetry, captured and sightings
messages.body_plain:
I’m fitting a somewhat unconventional
SECR model, and was wondering if I could get some advice. Sorry if this is
really long, it’s my first time asking for this kind of advice.

Study Description:

14 animals were live-captured and GPS collared over
the course of 7 months.
Collars were fitted with unique visual markers.
After capture/marking was complete, animals were exposed
for 2 months to 3 types of devices.
Devices were deactivated to prevent animal capture
(to protect the GPS collar) but ‘captures’ were recorded via camera monitoring:
this can be approximated as resighting data.

 The primary aim of the study is to calculate sigma
and capture probability. Density is secondary.

Modelling approach:

I’m using SECR 4.5.4. So far I’ve modelled this
data as a resighting study, using camera observations. However, I know my
marked animals are clustered, and I think I need to include their known
distribution.

I know I can do this using the mark-recapture data.
However, I’ve been avoiding that because 1) I have hundreds of capture nights spread
across chaotic field notes, and traps were shifted regularly. I could address
the shifting using usage but it would still be laborious and potentially a
little inaccurate. 2) The capture/marking period was so long (~7 months) that I
very much doubt it was a closed system.

I was thinking I could instead use the GPS data,
and this might have the additional benefit of improving sigma and g0 estimates.
However, it appears GPS data is not compatible with mark-resight (https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/secr-telemetry.pdf)
at least in secr 4.5. The info file mentions the caveat “except possibly in
distinct sessions (this has not been tested)”, but I’m not sure exactly what
this means: does this refer to when you are modelling only 1 session?

So I guess I’ve got three questions:

1)     Given I am primarily aiming for calculating sigma
and g0, and density is secondary, I think having the known distribution of marked
animals is more important than avoiding violating the closed-system assumption.
I’m not a statistician. Does that sound reasonable?

2)
Is GPS data
still incompatible with resighting data in 4.5.4? I am only modelling one
session, does that change things?

3)     Is there any other way I could use the GPS data or simplify
the capture/recapture data to add the known distribution of individuals? E.g.
using sigmas and home range centres calculated from GPS data?

Thank you for your help!

messages.body_plain:
Sorry if this is stated somewhere. I've looked but cannot find it.

I'm fitting a mark-resight model and know two of my marked animals left (dispersed from) the study sight during the resighting phase and did not return. Marked animals were fitted with GPS collars taking nightly fixes, so I know exactly what night they left on.

When dealing with sighting data, is there a way to indicate that an animal has left on the date in question, or is this a limitation of the model?

(I thought could perhaps use a negative occassion in the capture file (e.g. -12) to simulate them dying on the night of their most recent sighting, but this would be days before they actually left, and I'm not sure this works with resighting data.)

Cheers
Tess

messages.body_plain:
Hi Allan,

I think you want make.mask rather than read.mask. With a truncated version of your polygon and a made-up spacing, something like:

x <- c(380377,381874,383690,385729,387949,380377)
y <- c(7680086,7680245,7680002,7679496,7680458,7680086)
Mal_xy <- data.frame(x = x, y =y)
Mal_Mask <- make.mask(type = "polygon", poly = Mal_xy, spacing = 100)
plot(Mal_Mask)

Pretty sure read.mask doesn't use polygon arguments and these are just being ignored, so the data frame with the polygon outline gets used directly as mask points - that gives the error because all the interior points are missing.

Hope that helps,
Ian
